I would recommend doing a little research first on the different approaches to homeschooling and see if you can find one that works for you and your family and then learn more about it. Homeschoolers are a diverse group and there is a lot of info out there, and I find it can be overwhelming.

There is some overlap and you of course don't have to commit to one single approach, but having an idea of what you want allows you to find more targeted resources that align with your goals and values. Unschooling, Montessori, classical model, Abeka books, Charlotte Mason, etc.

We have found the Montessori approach to be great for little ones and helping them develop personal responsibility, confidence, and a sense of place in the world. Montessori From the Start by Paula Polk Lillard has a lot of great info for little ones even though I don't really like how it's organized. I'm sure you can find lots of good books at your local library, too.

For older kids, we are interested in pursuing the classical model in the future. The Well-Trained Mind by Susan Wise Bauer is the standard intro for this approach. It is academically rigorous but is something you can adapt and scale as needed.

I'll also add that it's worth considering when you want to start. It is common now for kids to start formal education very early. However, there is not a lot of evidence that it does much good. Allowing your child to learn through play and incorporating things like counting and basic math skills into everyday life is much more meaningful than worksheets and class for youngsters. We don't want a formal approach for our children until 7, except maybe a little bit of a basic phonics primer if needed.

Hope any of this is helpful! Good luck! The most important thing is that you just do it :)

We will be starting our 3rd year homeschooling. I have a differing range of ages with a lot of littles, but I try to maintain a "one-room schoolhouse" as much as possible, just for the ease of it. Each child has their own level for Math, reading/spelling, and writing expectations. I teach science, the arts, and history together. My oldest child is a few years ahead of the others, so I expect them to complete more in-depth work. We are going to be starting Latin this year, which we've never done, so we will see how it goes. They will also have a Bible verse for copywork.

We stick to a classical education. We began with a program called Classical Conversations, which is one where you meet up with a community one day a week for 24 weeks. We really love that curriculum, but because of various circumstances, will not be participating in a community, and doing at all at home this year. They cover 7 subjects: Math, History, Science, Latin, Timeline, English, Geography. We also learn about the Orchestra, classical composers, various artists, and artistic techniques.

The curriculum I have planned out for this year is:

Classical Conversation's "Foundations" (weekly memory work for 24 weeks) Saxon Math (I stick with the old school 1st or 2nd editions for each level, which you can find used for fairly cheap) Spell to Write and Read - I use it as all three for my beginning readers, and just for spelling/spelling rules for the older ones Cursive First (for the littles to learn handwriting) Institute of Excellence in Writing - Composition for the oldest -(ages 9-12) Essentials of the English Language (This is through Classical Conversations, and teaches all the grammar rules - for the 9-12 age set) Apologia's Exploring Creation (this year we're focusing on Astronomy) this includes science experiments Memoria Press's First Form Latin Mystery of History - this includes various activities as well.

We also plan to join a home school gym class with our local YMCA that meets once/week.

Now, with all this being said, I still feel like it's pretty ambitious, especially considering I'll be having a newborn in the midst of all of this. So, these plans will go forward if the Good Lord wills it. :) We shall see what the next year brings.

If you have any questions about anything, or where to find cheap used curriculum ask away, I've found some pretty good resources.

Don't forget to look into your state's homeschool laws, and get registered properly and on time so you don't have issues with truancy and that garbage breathing down your neck.
